question: Build an LRU cache with O(1) average-time get and put operations.
best_solution: Store key-to-node references in a hash map and order nodes in a doubly linked list. Move every accessed or updated node to the front. Evict the tail when capacity is exceeded. Use a sentinel head and tail to simplify pointer updates.
best_complexity: O(1) average time per operation; O(capacity) space
alternative_solution_1: Use Python OrderedDict and move_to_end after access; popitem(last=False) for eviction.
alternative_complexity_1: O(1) average operations in Python; O(capacity) space
alternative_1_tradeoff: Excellent production Python option, but it hides the linked-list mechanics an interviewer may want you to implement.
alternative_solution_2: Keep entries in a list and linearly search/move them on each operation.
alternative_complexity_2: O(n) get/put; O(capacity) space
alternative_2_tradeoff: Simpler but too slow as capacity grows.
edge_cases: Capacity zero; update existing key; repeated eviction; missing key; least-recently-used tie cases.
follow_up_questions: Add TTL expiry, thread safety, weighted capacity or persistence.

question: Design a tool-using agent that cannot make an irreversible purchase or delete data without approval.
skills_tested: Tool permissions; policy enforcement; idempotency; audit
best_solution: Separate planning from execution. Give each tool a typed schema and narrow capability. Enforce permissions outside the model. Require a short-lived approval token for high-impact actions. Use idempotency keys, audit logs, timeouts and post-action verification. Treat retrieved content as untrusted input.
best_complexity: Design: bounded authority, complete audit trail, explicit approval gate
alternative_solution_1: Require the model to follow a strict system prompt and ask itself whether an action is safe.
alternative_complexity_1: No enforceable complexity bound; safety depends on model behaviour
alternative_1_tradeoff: A prompt is useful guidance but cannot enforce permissions against prompt injection, model error or tool bugs.
alternative_solution_2: Require a human to approve every tool call, including harmless read-only actions.
alternative_complexity_2: High human latency; low automation throughput
alternative_2_tradeoff: Very safe but impractical; apply approval selectively according to impact and reversibility.
edge_cases: Prompt injection in retrieved pages; approval replay; duplicate requests; partial failures; revoked access; timeout after a side effect.
follow_up_questions: Add policy versioning, delegated approval, sandboxing and rollback plans.

question: Find the shortest path through a grid with blocked cells, moving in four directions.
best_solution: Treat each free cell as a vertex. Run BFS from the start, mark cells when enqueued, and store each cell's parent. Reconstruct the route by walking backward from the target. Return no path if the target is never reached.
best_complexity: O(rows × columns) time and space
alternative_solution_1: Use Dijkstra with every move assigned cost one.
alternative_complexity_1: O(V log V + E) with a typical heap implementation
alternative_1_tradeoff: Correct but does extra priority-queue work when all edges have equal weight.
alternative_solution_2: Use DFS and retain the shortest path found.
alternative_complexity_2: O(V + E) traversal, but worst-case path search may explore many routes
alternative_2_tradeoff: DFS does not guarantee that the first route is shortest; exhaustive shortest-path search can be expensive.
edge_cases: Blocked start/end; disconnected target; one-cell grid; repeated visits; rectangular grids.
follow_up_questions: Add diagonal moves, terrain costs or moving obstacles.

question: Design an evaluation to test whether a robot policy generalises to homes and objects it never saw during training.
skills_tested: Robotics evaluation; data leakage; distribution shift
best_solution: Split data by entire environment, object instance and task family. Hold out combinations, not just frames. Measure task completion, collisions, recovery, intervention and time. Repeat across seeds and report uncertainty. Keep a hidden test set and log policy versions.
best_complexity: Evaluation: stratified held-out environments; confidence intervals for key rates
alternative_solution_1: Randomly split camera frames from each recorded episode into train and test sets.
alternative_complexity_1: Low apparent evaluation cost
alternative_1_tradeoff: Near-duplicate frames from the same room and episode leak into both sets, exaggerating generalisation.
alternative_solution_2: Use domain randomisation during training and test on randomly generated scenes.
alternative_complexity_2: Useful robustness training; not a substitute for a fixed held-out benchmark
alternative_2_tradeoff: Random scenes may not represent real deployment, and training randomisation can leak into evaluation if not separated.
edge_cases: New room layouts; lighting shifts; unseen object shapes; sensor dropout; rare failures; sim-to-real gap.
follow_up_questions: Add blinded human ratings and cross-robot transfer tests.

question: Merge a list of overlapping time intervals into a minimal set of non-overlapping intervals.
best_solution: Sort intervals by start. Add the first interval to the output. For each next interval, merge it with the final output interval when they overlap; otherwise append it. State clearly whether touching endpoints count as overlap.
best_complexity: O(n log n) time; O(n) output space
alternative_solution_1: Use a sweep line over sorted start and end events.
alternative_complexity_1: O(n log n) time; O(n) space
alternative_1_tradeoff: Useful when the task expands to counts or active-set queries, but more bookkeeping for simple merging.
alternative_solution_2: Compare and merge every pair repeatedly until no overlap remains.
alternative_complexity_2: O(n²) or worse depending on implementation
alternative_2_tradeoff: Repeated rescanning is harder to reason about and scales poorly.
edge_cases: Empty input; nested intervals; duplicates; touching endpoints; negative coordinates; reversed intervals.
follow_up_questions: Return merged interval lengths or handle streaming arrivals.

question: Build an evaluation that detects when an AI system games a reward metric while missing the user's real goal.
skills_tested: Reward hacking; evaluation design; adversarial testing
best_solution: Write the intended behaviour as observable invariants. Create adversarial tasks where the proxy score can be maximised without completing the real task. Score task success, constraint violations and user intent independently. Use held-out attacks, trace review and regression tests for each exploit.
best_complexity: Evaluation: exploit rate, task success and false-positive rate measured separately
alternative_solution_1: Collect more examples and optimise the existing reward score harder.
alternative_complexity_1: Training cost grows with dataset and model size
alternative_1_tradeoff: More optimisation against the same proxy can intensify the exploit instead of fixing the objective.
alternative_solution_2: Use human review as the only evaluation method.
alternative_complexity_2: High cost per example; slow feedback
alternative_2_tradeoff: Human review is valuable for ambiguous cases but inconsistent and difficult to scale alone.
edge_cases: Metric loopholes; hidden side effects; evaluator leakage; reward-model disagreement; distribution shift.
follow_up_questions: Add causal tests, independent graders and runtime action constraints.

question: Return the top K items from a large feed using a relevance score and a recency signal.
best_solution: Filter ineligible items first. Compute the documented score and keep the best K in a min-heap of size K. Add a deterministic tie-breaker. Apply diversity constraints in a final re-ranking pass.
best_complexity: O(n log K) time; O(K) heap space
alternative_solution_1: Sort all items and take the first K.
alternative_complexity_1: O(n log n) time; O(n) space
alternative_1_tradeoff: Very readable and often fine for small feeds, but wastes work when K is small.
alternative_solution_2: Use Quickselect to find the Kth score, then sort only the selected items.
alternative_complexity_2: O(n) average selection plus O(K log K) sort; O(n) or in-place space
alternative_2_tradeoff: Fast on average but has less predictable worst-case behaviour and needs careful tie handling.
edge_cases: Ties; missing scores; blocked content; duplicate authors; K zero or larger than input.
follow_up_questions: Add freshness decay, diversity quotas and online experiment metrics.

question: Design a high-traffic feed ranking system that balances relevance, freshness, creator diversity and latency.
best_solution: Use candidate generation, eligibility filtering, feature retrieval, ranking and constrained re-ranking. Track each objective separately. Enforce diversity and freshness constraints after scoring. Cache stable features, set timeouts and fall back to a safe ranking when dependencies fail. Experiment with guardrail metrics.
best_complexity: System design: explicit latency SLOs and separate quality/diversity guardrails
alternative_solution_1: Combine every signal into one opaque weighted score and rank once.
alternative_complexity_1: Low initial complexity
alternative_1_tradeoff: A single score hides trade-offs and makes diversity, fairness and debugging difficult.
alternative_solution_2: Use hand-written chronological and category rules only.
alternative_complexity_2: Very low scoring cost
alternative_2_tradeoff: Rules are predictable but often miss personal relevance and can become brittle as content grows.
edge_cases: Cold-start creators; spam; feedback loops; stale features; dependency timeouts; sudden traffic spikes.
follow_up_questions: Explain exploration, creator fairness and online/offline metric drift.

question: Make a job-processing endpoint safe when clients retry the same request after a timeout.
best_solution: Require an idempotency key. Store the key, request hash and result in durable storage in the same transaction as the job state change. On retry, return the stored result; reject reuse of the key with a different request.
best_complexity: O(1) average key lookup; storage proportional to retained keys
alternative_solution_1: Make the business operation naturally idempotent, for example set status to a target value rather than incrementing it.
alternative_complexity_1: Usually O(1) per update
alternative_1_tradeoff: Excellent when the operation can be expressed as setting state, but not possible for every external side effect.
alternative_solution_2: Acquire a distributed lock before processing the request.
alternative_complexity_2: Lock coordination cost depends on the store
alternative_2_tradeoff: Locks help coordinate concurrent requests but do not alone resolve crashes after an external side effect.
edge_cases: Same key and same payload; same key with changed payload; timeout after commit; concurrent retries; key expiry.
follow_up_questions: Add an outbox for reliable external notifications.

question: Design a multi-tenant storage service with strict tenant isolation and regional failover.
best_solution: Derive tenant identity from trusted authentication, not request parameters. Enforce authorisation on every operation. Partition or namespace tenant data, encrypt it, audit access, and test cross-tenant denial. Replicate with versioned writes, fencing and documented recovery objectives.
best_complexity: System design: specify RPO/RTO, consistency and isolation invariants
alternative_solution_1: Use a shared database and rely on every caller to send the correct tenant ID.
alternative_complexity_1: Low operational cost
alternative_1_tradeoff: Caller-supplied tenant IDs are not proof of access and can expose another tenant's data.
alternative_solution_2: Give each tenant a separate database and region.
alternative_complexity_2: Strong isolation; operational cost grows with tenant count
alternative_2_tradeoff: Isolation is strong but provisioning, migrations, backups and failover become expensive at large scale.
edge_cases: Tenant ID spoofing; noisy neighbours; region outage; stale replicas; key rotation; partial failover.
follow_up_questions: Compare pooled, siloed and hybrid tenancy models.

question: Implement a rate limiter that allows short bursts but controls the long-term request rate.
best_solution: Track tokens and last-refill time. Add elapsed time × refill rate up to bucket capacity. Allow a request only when a token is available, then subtract one. Use a monotonic clock and atomic updates.
best_complexity: O(1) time and state per key
alternative_solution_1: Use a sliding-window counter with two adjacent time buckets.
alternative_complexity_1: O(1) state per key
alternative_1_tradeoff: Memory-efficient and smoother than a fixed window, but only approximates an exact sliding window.
alternative_solution_2: Keep every request timestamp in a sliding-window log.
alternative_complexity_2: O(log n) or O(1) amortised update depending on data structure; O(requests in window) space
alternative_2_tradeoff: More exact but stores many events and consumes more memory at high traffic.
edge_cases: Clock jumps; concurrent requests; burst at capacity; multiple server instances; key expiry.
follow_up_questions: Make it distributed using Redis or sharded counters.

question: Design a durable queue and worker system with retries, dead-letter handling and duplicate delivery.
best_solution: Persist messages before acknowledging producers. Lease messages to workers using visibility timeouts. Retry transient errors with capped exponential backoff and jitter. Send poison messages to a dead-letter queue. Make handlers idempotent and measure queue age, retry count and processing latency.
best_complexity: System design: at-least-once delivery plus idempotent effects
alternative_solution_1: Use a relational jobs table with workers polling rows and claiming them transactionally.
alternative_complexity_1: Simple deployment; database load depends on polling rate
alternative_1_tradeoff: Good for moderate throughput, but frequent polling and row contention limit scale.
alternative_solution_2: Use a streaming log with consumer offsets.
alternative_complexity_2: High throughput; operational complexity depends on broker
alternative_2_tradeoff: Excellent for ordered replay and high volume, but more complex than a task queue for independent jobs.
edge_cases: Worker crash after side effect; poison messages; ordering; duplicate delivery; backlog surge; poison queue replay.
follow_up_questions: Explain outbox/inbox patterns and exactly-once side-effect limits.

question: Explain and implement tiled matrix multiplication for a GPU.
best_solution: Partition output into tiles. Load input tiles cooperatively into shared memory, synchronise, accumulate multiply-adds in registers and write each output once. Tune tile sizes against shared-memory and register limits; benchmark occupancy and memory traffic.
best_complexity: O(MNK) arithmetic; lower global-memory traffic through reuse
alternative_solution_1: Use a naive kernel that loads both matrix values directly from global memory for every multiply.
alternative_complexity_1: O(MNK) arithmetic; simple implementation
alternative_1_tradeoff: Useful correctness baseline, but repeated global-memory loads waste bandwidth.
alternative_solution_2: Call an optimised vendor library such as cuBLAS.
alternative_complexity_2: Typically highly optimised; exact performance is library and hardware dependent
alternative_2_tradeoff: Best production default, but hides kernel-level implementation and tuning concepts.
edge_cases: Non-divisible dimensions; alignment; precision; memory coalescing; tile limits; numerical error.
follow_up_questions: Add mixed precision and compare throughput/accuracy.

question: Design an LLM inference scheduler for variable prompt lengths under a strict GPU KV-cache budget.
best_solution: Separate prefill and decode scheduling. Use continuous batching, paged KV-cache blocks, token-aware admission and per-request limits. Track memory before admission; pre-empt or reject safely under pressure. Measure throughput and p95/p99 latency on mixed sequence lengths.
best_complexity: System design: memory bounded by active token blocks
alternative_solution_1: Use a fixed batch size and reserve the maximum context length for every request.
alternative_complexity_1: Predictable but wasteful memory use
alternative_1_tradeoff: Short requests waste reserved KV-cache space; large context limits reduce concurrency.
alternative_solution_2: Process one request at a time with no batching.
alternative_complexity_2: Low scheduler complexity; lowest concurrency
alternative_2_tradeoff: Avoids batch interference but wastes accelerator capacity and reduces throughput.
edge_cases: Long prompts; memory fragmentation; cancellation; starvation; fairness; prefill/decode imbalance.
follow_up_questions: Add speculative decoding and admission control by service tier.

question: Implement a fixed-size ring buffer for a continuous stream of sensor readings.
best_solution: Keep a fixed array, write index and item count. Insert at the write index, advance modulo capacity and cap the count. Read oldest-first by modular offsets. Explicitly define whether a full buffer overwrites or rejects.
best_complexity: O(1) insert; O(1) indexed read; O(capacity) memory
alternative_solution_1: Use a deque with a maximum length.
alternative_complexity_1: O(1) append/pop at ends; O(capacity) memory
alternative_1_tradeoff: Safer and simpler in high-level code, but less control over fixed memory and embedded layout.
alternative_solution_2: Append to a list and periodically delete old readings.
alternative_complexity_2: O(1) append; O(n) shifts or cleanup
alternative_2_tradeoff: Unbounded growth between cleanups and occasional latency spikes make it less suitable for real-time use.
edge_cases: Capacity zero/one; wraparound; overwrite policy; concurrent reader/writer; stale samples.
follow_up_questions: Add lock-free single-producer/single-consumer semantics.

question: Choose and deploy an on-device model under memory, power and latency limits without losing too much accuracy.
best_solution: Measure a baseline on target hardware. Quantise using representative calibration data, validate on held-out data, then profile memory, energy and tail latency. Apply pruning or distillation only if quantisation misses the budget. Check operator support and thermal throttling.
best_complexity: Evaluation: model size, peak RAM, energy per inference and p95 latency
alternative_solution_1: Prune weights or channels and fine-tune the smaller model.
alternative_complexity_1: Savings depend on structured sparsity and hardware kernels
alternative_1_tradeoff: Unstructured sparsity may not translate into real speedups on the target device.
alternative_solution_2: Distil a smaller student model from a larger teacher.
alternative_complexity_2: Training cost upfront; efficient runtime if successful
alternative_2_tradeoff: Can retain accuracy but requires suitable teacher data and additional training.
edge_cases: Calibration mismatch; unsupported operators; battery state; thermal throttling; worst-case input size.
follow_up_questions: Compare int8, int4 and mixed-precision deployment.

question: Design a job state machine that recovers safely after a worker crashes.
best_solution: Persist queued, running, succeeded and failed states. Acquire a lease before processing, checkpoint progress, and use conditional versioned updates for transitions. A recovery worker reclaims expired leases and resumes from the last safe checkpoint.
best_complexity: O(1) average state transition; O(number of jobs) storage
alternative_solution_1: Use a transactional database row with SELECT FOR UPDATE and status checks.
alternative_complexity_1: Database lock cost depends on contention
alternative_1_tradeoff: Reliable and simple for moderate workloads, but long-held locks reduce throughput.
alternative_solution_2: Keep job state only in worker memory and replay on restart.
alternative_complexity_2: Fast while process lives; no durable state
alternative_2_tradeoff: A crash destroys progress and can duplicate side effects.
edge_cases: Worker dies before/after side effect; expired lease; stale worker resumes; duplicate completion.
follow_up_questions: Add an outbox, fencing token and compensation step.

question: Design identity and permission controls for autonomous agents that access enterprise tools.
best_solution: Give each agent a distinct verifiable identity. Exchange it for short-lived scoped credentials. Authorise every action using agent, user, task and resource context. Log decisions, separate read/write/approve roles and support rapid revocation.
best_complexity: System design: every action is attributable and checked
alternative_solution_1: Use a shared service account for all agents and rotate its key regularly.
alternative_complexity_1: Low setup effort
alternative_1_tradeoff: A shared account removes attribution, weakens least privilege and complicates incident response.
alternative_solution_2: Issue long-lived credentials per agent.
alternative_complexity_2: Simple runtime authentication
alternative_2_tradeoff: Long-lived credentials increase exposure after compromise and make revocation slow.
edge_cases: Prompt injection; agent delegation; stale tokens; stolen credentials; emergency revocation; audit gaps.
follow_up_questions: Add workload identity federation and policy simulation.

question: Split a dataset into train and test sets without leaking exact or near-duplicate examples.
best_solution: Normalise records, hash exact duplicates, cluster near-duplicates with a similarity index, then assign entire groups to one split. Record dataset version, grouping logic and random seed.
best_complexity: O(n) exact hashing; near-duplicate cost depends on similarity index
alternative_solution_1: Use stratified random splitting after exact deduplication.
alternative_complexity_1: O(n) plus sorting or sampling
alternative_1_tradeoff: Good baseline for class balance, but it will still leak semantic near-duplicates if grouping is incomplete.
alternative_solution_2: Use time-based splitting.
alternative_complexity_2: O(n log n) if sorting by time
alternative_2_tradeoff: Best when deployment predicts the future, but can create class imbalance or omit rare groups.
edge_cases: Duplicate text with formatting changes; same author; same source; label imbalance; temporal drift.
follow_up_questions: Add group-aware cross-validation and leakage audits.

question: Design a model inference API with dynamic batching that does not let long requests starve short ones.
best_solution: Queue requests with deadlines and token estimates. Batch compatible requests up to size and wait-time limits. Enforce per-tenant quotas, reject overload early and report queue wait separately from execution time. Cancel queued work when clients disconnect where safe.
best_complexity: System design: bounded queue; p95/p99 latency and throughput metrics
alternative_solution_1: Use a fixed batch size and wait until it fills before inference.
alternative_complexity_1: Easy to implement
alternative_1_tradeoff: Low traffic waits too long for a full batch, harming latency.
alternative_solution_2: Use one request per GPU worker with independent queues.
alternative_complexity_2: Simple fairness model; lower batching efficiency
alternative_2_tradeoff: Prevents batch interference but reduces GPU utilisation and throughput.
edge_cases: Large prompt; burst traffic; client cancellation; slow tenant; incompatible model versions.
follow_up_questions: Add deadline-aware scheduling and priority classes.

question: Count distinct users in event-time windows when events can arrive late or more than once.
best_solution: Deduplicate by stable event ID, use event timestamps for window assignment, and set a watermark to bound late-event correction. Persist checkpoints and document how records arriving after the watermark are handled.
best_complexity: State proportional to active windows and deduplication horizon
alternative_solution_1: Process events in periodic batch jobs and recompute each window from stored data.
alternative_complexity_1: Cost depends on volume and retention
alternative_1_tradeoff: Simpler and often more accurate for small data, but slower and more expensive for frequent updates.
alternative_solution_2: Deduplicate only in worker memory and aggregate by arrival time.
alternative_complexity_2: O(1) local lookup; state lost on restart
alternative_2_tradeoff: Incorrect with delayed events and restarts; results vary across workers.
edge_cases: Duplicate IDs; out-of-order data; very late events; daylight-saving boundaries; restart recovery.
follow_up_questions: Explain exactly-once processing claims and checkpoint recovery.

question: Design a feature pipeline that supports historical backfills while keeping online and offline features consistent.
best_solution: Use versioned transformations across batch and streaming paths. Store event and ingestion time. Enforce point-in-time joins, record input versions and lineage, make backfills idempotent, and monitor online/offline skew.
best_complexity: System design: reproducible features and bounded freshness lag
alternative_solution_1: Maintain separate online and offline transformation implementations and compare outputs nightly.
alternative_complexity_1: Low coupling between systems
alternative_1_tradeoff: The implementations drift and only detect skew after it occurs.
alternative_solution_2: Compute features on demand from raw data for both paths.
alternative_complexity_2: One source of truth; request latency depends on raw-data query
alternative_2_tradeoff: Strong consistency conceptually, but usually too slow and costly for online inference.
edge_cases: Late events; schema evolution; backfill overlaps live writes; point-in-time leakage; deleted records.
follow_up_questions: Add feature versioning and rollback.

question: Design a tenant-safe vector search endpoint over customer documents.
best_solution: Authenticate the caller, derive tenant identity from trusted credentials, and enforce a mandatory tenant filter before ranking results. Audit access and test that client-supplied tenant IDs cannot access another tenant's index.
best_complexity: Index cost depends on vector count and search method; tenant isolation is invariant
alternative_solution_1: Keep a physically separate vector index for each tenant.
alternative_complexity_1: Query isolation is simple; storage/operations scale with tenant count
alternative_1_tradeoff: Strong isolation but costly for many small tenants and difficult to manage at scale.
alternative_solution_2: Search a shared index and filter results in the client.
alternative_complexity_2: Potentially fast initial implementation
alternative_2_tradeoff: Client-side filtering can leak data and should never be the security boundary.
edge_cases: Forged tenant ID; deleted tenant; empty index; stale permissions; index rebuild.
follow_up_questions: Compare shared, partitioned and dedicated-index approaches.

question: Design a global task service that survives a regional outage without executing the same external action twice.
best_solution: Store durable replicated task records with unique IDs and versioned leases. Define ownership using a single-writer or consensus-backed rule. On failover, use fencing tokens so stale workers cannot commit. Make external effects idempotent and state RPO/RTO trade-offs.
best_complexity: System design: explicit consistency and recovery guarantees
alternative_solution_1: Use active-active workers in every region and let them race to claim tasks.
alternative_complexity_1: High availability; no central bottleneck
alternative_1_tradeoff: Without consensus or fencing, two regions can perform the same side effect.
alternative_solution_2: Use a primary region with a warm standby and manual failover.
alternative_complexity_2: Simpler consistency model; higher recovery time
alternative_2_tradeoff: Reduces split-brain risk but availability is lower during a regional outage.
edge_cases: Network partition; stale lease; replay; delayed replication; external API timeout.
follow_up_questions: Explain CAP trade-offs and compensation for non-idempotent actions.

question: Given CI jobs and dependencies, return a valid execution order or report a cycle.
best_solution: Build adjacency lists and indegrees. Run Kahn's algorithm with a queue of zero-indegree jobs. Decrement dependants as jobs are emitted. If fewer than all jobs are emitted, the dependency graph contains a cycle.
best_complexity: O(V + E) time and space
alternative_solution_1: Use DFS with three-colour marking to detect back edges and create reverse postorder.
alternative_complexity_1: O(V + E) time and space
alternative_1_tradeoff: Also linear and useful when recursive traversal or explicit cycle path is desired.
alternative_solution_2: Try every possible job ordering until dependencies are satisfied.
alternative_complexity_2: O(V! × checks) worst case
alternative_2_tradeoff: Exponential and unnecessary for a DAG ordering problem.
edge_cases: No jobs; disconnected graph; duplicate edge; self-dependency; multiple valid orders.
follow_up_questions: Prioritise ready jobs by duration or critical path.

question: Design a CI runner system that safely executes untrusted pull-request code at scale.
best_solution: Use ephemeral isolated runners with least-privilege tokens, no production secrets, restricted network egress and disposable workspaces. Pin actions by immutable commit, verify artifacts and separate trusted workflows from untrusted fork workflows.
best_complexity: System design: isolation boundary and secret-exposure tests
alternative_solution_1: Use persistent self-hosted runners and clean the workspace after each job.
alternative_complexity_1: Lower provisioning overhead
alternative_1_tradeoff: Malicious code can persist outside the workspace, inspect host state or steal available credentials.
alternative_solution_2: Run every job in a fresh virtual machine with strict policy.
alternative_complexity_2: Strong isolation; higher startup and infrastructure cost
alternative_2_tradeoff: Secure default, but may be expensive for short jobs; pool pre-warmed isolated VMs if needed.
edge_cases: Fork PR; poisoned cache; malicious dependency; artifact tampering; credential exfiltration; runner compromise.
follow_up_questions: Add provenance attestations and workload identity.

question: Plan a collision-free path for a robot arm through a simple obstacle field.
best_solution: Represent valid robot configurations in a collision-checked graph or discretised configuration space. Run A* with an admissible heuristic and reconstruct the path. Validate the smoothed path against collision geometry before execution.
best_complexity: A* depends on graph size; worst-case exponential in path depth
alternative_solution_1: Use Dijkstra with collision-free edges.
alternative_complexity_1: O((V + E) log V) with a heap
alternative_1_tradeoff: Optimal for non-negative edge costs but explores more nodes without a heuristic.
alternative_solution_2: Use a potential-field planner that moves away from obstacles and toward the goal.
alternative_complexity_2: Fast local computation
alternative_2_tradeoff: Can get stuck in local minima and may oscillate near narrow passages.
edge_cases: Narrow corridors; moving obstacles; joint limits; self-collision; unreachable goal.
follow_up_questions: Add trajectory timing and torque limits.

question: Design a manipulation policy that moves from simulation to real objects without unsafe contact.
best_solution: Train across varied physical parameters, textures and object geometry; use domain randomisation with realistic calibration. Add force/torque limits, collision monitoring and a low-level safe controller. Validate first in simulation, then in staged real-world trials with a rollback policy.
best_complexity: Evaluation: success, damage, contact-force and intervention rates
alternative_solution_1: Use a policy trained only on one high-fidelity simulation.
alternative_complexity_1: Less training variability
alternative_1_tradeoff: Small simulator errors in friction, compliance or sensing can cause large real-world failures.
alternative_solution_2: Use hand-coded motion primitives for every object.
alternative_complexity_2: Predictable for known objects
alternative_2_tradeoff: Does not generalise well to unknown shapes and contact conditions.
edge_cases: Unexpected mass; slippery surface; camera occlusion; force sensor dropout; human proximity.
follow_up_questions: Add online system identification with strict safety bounds.

question: Estimate a moving obstacle's future position and plan a safe robot route around it.
best_solution: Fuse sensor observations into a tracked position/velocity estimate. Predict a short horizon, inflate obstacle geometry by uncertainty and robot footprint, then replan using a time-aware graph search.
best_complexity: Perception and planning cost depends on tracks and map resolution
alternative_solution_1: Use a constant-velocity Kalman filter plus a static A* map update.
alternative_complexity_1: Kalman update is O(d³) for state dimension d; A* depends on map size
alternative_1_tradeoff: Good simple baseline but a static map can miss time-dependent crossing conflicts.
alternative_solution_2: Use reactive potential fields around current obstacle positions.
alternative_complexity_2: Low per-step computation
alternative_2_tradeoff: Fast but may oscillate or fail in narrow passages and does not reason about future occupancy.
edge_cases: Occlusion; sudden stop; crossing paths; sensor delay; prediction uncertainty.
follow_up_questions: Add multi-agent prediction and safe stopping distance.

question: Design a balance controller for a biped robot recovering from an unexpected push.
best_solution: Estimate body state and contact forces. Use a model-predictive controller to choose feasible foot placement and body motion while respecting friction and joint limits. Keep a fast stabilising low-level controller and a safe fall/recovery mode.
best_complexity: Control complexity depends on optimisation horizon and model size
alternative_solution_1: Use a linear inverted-pendulum model with capture-point foot placement.
alternative_complexity_1: Small optimisation or closed-form step target
alternative_1_tradeoff: Fast and interpretable but less accurate for large motions and complex contact changes.
alternative_solution_2: Use a learned end-to-end policy from simulation.
alternative_complexity_2: Inference can be fast; training/evaluation cost is high
alternative_2_tradeoff: May generalise poorly outside training and can be hard to certify without a safety layer.
edge_cases: Push during single support; slippery floor; actuator saturation; delayed state estimate.
follow_up_questions: Explain whole-body control and contact switching.

question: Choose a safe robot skill when the task state is uncertain and multiple skills may apply.
best_solution: Estimate task state and skill confidence. Select a skill only when preconditions and safety checks pass; otherwise request more sensing or use a safe fallback. Log the decision and use hysteresis to avoid rapid skill switching.
best_complexity: O(number of skills) scoring; safety checks dominate
alternative_solution_1: Choose the highest-scoring skill from a learned classifier.
alternative_complexity_1: O(number of skills) inference
alternative_1_tradeoff: Simple but ignores uncertainty calibration and can choose a high-score unsafe skill.
alternative_solution_2: Use a hand-authored decision tree.
alternative_complexity_2: O(depth) evaluation
alternative_2_tradeoff: Transparent but brittle in new environments and hard to maintain as skills grow.
edge_cases: Ambiguous state; all skills low confidence; conflicting preconditions; sensor outage.
follow_up_questions: Add risk-sensitive selection and runtime monitors.

question: Design a robot foundation policy that transfers across different robot bodies without unsafe actions.
best_solution: Condition the policy on robot morphology, actuator limits and sensor configuration. Map actions through a validated embodiment-specific controller. Train across diverse robots and tasks, then evaluate on held-out morphologies with action constraints and recovery monitors.
best_complexity: Evaluation: transfer success, constraint violations and recovery rate
alternative_solution_1: Train a separate policy for each robot.
alternative_complexity_1: Simpler optimisation and specialised control
alternative_1_tradeoff: Poor transfer and duplicated data/training effort.
alternative_solution_2: Train one shared policy without telling it which robot body is active.
alternative_complexity_2: One model to maintain
alternative_2_tradeoff: The same command can have different meaning and safety on different actuators and kinematics.
edge_cases: Joint-limit mismatch; missing sensors; actuator delay; unseen morphology; sim-to-real.
follow_up_questions: Add adapters and few-shot calibration.

question: Control a robot with a vision-language-action model while correcting mistakes from camera feedback.
best_solution: Encode the current image and instruction, predict a short action chunk, execute only a limited portion, observe again and replan. Keep action bounds and an independent stop condition. Measure task success and intervention.
best_complexity: Closed-loop cost depends on perception and policy inference frequency
alternative_solution_1: Predict a full open-loop action sequence and execute it without observing again.
alternative_complexity_1: Fewer inference calls
alternative_1_tradeoff: Efficient but errors accumulate when objects move or the model's first plan is wrong.
alternative_solution_2: Use a symbolic planner with hand-written motion primitives.
alternative_complexity_2: More interpretable; engineering effort grows with task set
alternative_2_tradeoff: Reliable in a narrow domain but weak on unanticipated object/task combinations.
edge_cases: Camera occlusion; moved object; grasp slip; ambiguous command; delayed observation.
follow_up_questions: Add uncertainty-triggered replanning and recovery skills.

question: Build a robot-learning dataset that captures rare failures without overfitting to one lab setup.
skills_tested: Data curation; active learning; robotics evaluation
best_solution: Stratify by task, object, environment and failure type. Preserve complete episodes and metadata. Sample rare failures deliberately, use active learning to request uncertain cases, and hold out environments and object instances for evaluation.
best_complexity: Data pipeline cost is linear in retained episodes plus indexing
alternative_solution_1: Collect uniformly random successful demonstrations.
alternative_complexity_1: Simple collection and storage
alternative_1_tradeoff: Rare failures remain underrepresented and the policy appears safer than it is.
alternative_solution_2: Generate all rare cases synthetically.
alternative_complexity_2: Low-cost scale for controllable variables
alternative_2_tradeoff: Synthetic data may not reflect real contact, sensor and human behaviour.
edge_cases: Sensor dropout; mislabeled success; repeated demonstrator; rare collision; domain shift.
follow_up_questions: Add human review and uncertainty-aware sampling.

question: Allocate delivery tasks to a fleet of robots using distance, battery and deadline constraints.
best_solution: Build a cost matrix for robot-task pairs using distance, battery penalty and deadline risk. Solve a minimum-cost assignment with Hungarian algorithm for a moderate dense fleet; reject infeasible pairs before solving.
best_complexity: O(n³) for square Hungarian assignment
alternative_solution_1: Use greedy nearest-robot assignment.
alternative_complexity_1: O(nm log n) depending on sorting
alternative_1_tradeoff: Fast and easy but can make locally good choices that cause poor fleet-wide allocations.
alternative_solution_2: Use min-cost max-flow for capacities and more complex constraints.
alternative_complexity_2: Polynomial; depends on graph size
alternative_2_tradeoff: More flexible but more implementation and runtime complexity than basic assignment.
edge_cases: No feasible robot; battery threshold; deadline ties; robot offline; task cancellation.
follow_up_questions: Add rolling-horizon re-planning and charging tasks.

question: Design a biped locomotion recovery system that detects and responds to a possible fall.
skills_tested: Gait control; state estimation; safety monitors
best_solution: Estimate centre of mass, foot contacts and body orientation. Detect instability with predictive margins, slow or stop unsafe actions, choose a feasible recovery step and retain a protective fall response. Test on perturbation suites with force and joint limits.
best_complexity: Control cost depends on state estimator and optimisation horizon
alternative_solution_1: Use threshold alarms on body tilt and trigger an emergency stop.
alternative_complexity_1: O(1) threshold check
alternative_1_tradeoff: Useful last-resort monitor but reacts after instability may already be difficult to recover.
alternative_solution_2: Train a reinforcement-learning recovery policy end to end.
alternative_complexity_2: Fast policy inference; expensive training and validation
alternative_2_tradeoff: Can perform well in simulation but needs robust transfer testing and an independent safety envelope.
edge_cases: Sensor drift; slippery floor; unexpected payload; actuator saturation; delayed contact detection.
follow_up_questions: Add predictive stability and recovery-step optimisation.

question: Schedule jobs across multiple industrial robots while avoiding shared-resource conflicts.
best_solution: Model jobs, robot capability, precedence and shared-zone constraints. Use a constraint solver or mixed-integer model for small/medium instances; validate every schedule against collision and resource rules.
best_complexity: Optimisation is NP-hard in general; solver performance depends on instance
alternative_solution_1: Use priority rules such as earliest deadline first with conflict checks.
alternative_complexity_1: O(n log n) sorting plus conflict checks
alternative_1_tradeoff: Fast baseline but can produce avoidable idle time and suboptimal makespan.
alternative_solution_2: Use greedy list scheduling with local swaps.
alternative_complexity_2: Usually fast; local-search cost depends on iterations
alternative_2_tradeoff: Often improves a simple heuristic but does not guarantee a global optimum.
edge_cases: Incompatible tool; shared workspace; job precedence; robot downtime; deadline conflict.
follow_up_questions: Add robust scheduling under uncertain task duration.

question: Coordinate several robots sharing a workspace while maintaining collision and safety constraints.
best_solution: Plan paths in space-time, reserve shared zones and check swept volumes. Use priority planning for a fast baseline, then resolve conflicts with a central optimiser or conflict-based search for smaller fleets. Add emergency stop zones and validate trajectories at execution.
best_complexity: Depends on search space; multi-agent pathfinding can be exponential
alternative_solution_1: Plan each robot path independently and run a collision checker afterward.
alternative_complexity_1: Single-robot paths are cheaper; collision check depends on path lengths
alternative_1_tradeoff: Detects conflicts but cannot guarantee a conflict-free schedule without re-planning.
alternative_solution_2: Serialize all robots so only one moves at a time.
alternative_complexity_2: Simple safety argument
alternative_2_tradeoff: Throughput collapses and may fail production targets.
edge_cases: Deadlock; narrow passage; delayed robot; payload size; human entering zone.
follow_up_questions: Add dynamic re-planning and safety-rated monitored stop.

question: Build a reliable data pipeline that validates, deduplicates and loads daily business records.
best_solution: Load into a staging area, validate schema and business rules, deduplicate by stable keys, then merge transactionally into the target. Record batch IDs, rejected rows and checksums. Make reruns idempotent.
best_complexity: O(n) expected with indexed keys; storage depends on batch
alternative_solution_1: Use an append-only event log and materialise clean tables downstream.
alternative_complexity_1: Ingestion O(n); query cost depends on materialisation
alternative_1_tradeoff: Good lineage and replay, but requires additional storage and consumer management.
alternative_solution_2: Update the target table directly row by row.
alternative_complexity_2: Low staging overhead
alternative_2_tradeoff: Partial failures leave mixed state and make rollback or audit difficult.
edge_cases: Duplicate batch; schema change; malformed row; late arrival; partial load.
follow_up_questions: Add data contracts, lineage and reconciliation reports.

question: Find the likely root cause of a production incident using logs, metrics and distributed traces.
best_solution: Normalise timestamps and trace IDs, correlate events across services, compare symptoms against a healthy baseline, and build a dependency graph. Rank hypotheses with supporting and contradicting evidence; preserve uncertainty and verify with a controlled test.
best_complexity: Pipeline cost roughly O(events + graph edges) plus indexing
alternative_solution_1: Search logs for frequent error strings and rank by count.
alternative_complexity_1: O(n) scan if unindexed; indexed search is faster
alternative_1_tradeoff: Finds common symptoms but can miss a rare upstream cause and confound noise with causality.
alternative_solution_2: Use a black-box anomaly detector over metrics.
alternative_complexity_2: Inference cost depends on model
alternative_2_tradeoff: Good for alerting but usually cannot explain causal relationships alone.
edge_cases: Clock skew; missing trace IDs; sampling; cascading failures; deploy correlation.
follow_up_questions: Add incident timeline and change-point detection.

question: Fuse noisy position measurements from two sensors into a smoother estimate.
best_solution: Define state and measurement models, predict state and covariance, then update with the new measurement and its noise covariance. Check innovation and gate outliers. Tune noise from calibration data.
best_complexity: O(d³) per update for a dense d-dimensional state; often lower for structured models
alternative_solution_1: Use a complementary filter with high-frequency data from one sensor and low-frequency correction from another.
alternative_complexity_1: O(1) per update for fixed-size state
alternative_1_tradeoff: Very efficient and easy to tune for simple systems, but models sensor noise less fully.
alternative_solution_2: Use a particle filter with weighted samples.
alternative_complexity_2: O(number of particles × measurement cost)
alternative_2_tradeoff: Handles nonlinear/non-Gaussian distributions but is more computationally expensive and can suffer particle depletion.
edge_cases: Sensor dropout; different sample rates; outliers; timestamp skew; coordinate mismatch.
follow_up_questions: Add delayed-measurement handling and sensor health monitoring.

question: Design a fail-safe embedded controller for a safety-critical device when a sensor or actuator becomes unreliable.
skills_tested: Real-time systems; fault detection; safety engineering
best_solution: Define hazards and safe states. Monitor sensor plausibility, actuator feedback, deadlines and watchdogs. Use bounded state transitions, redundant sensing where justified, independent shutdown paths and diagnostic logs. Test injected faults and timing overruns.
best_complexity: Design: bounded worst-case execution time and verified safety transitions
alternative_solution_1: Retry the failed sensor or actuator command until it succeeds.
alternative_complexity_1: Low normal-path complexity
alternative_1_tradeoff: Retries can hide a persistent fault, exceed real-time deadlines and repeat dangerous actions.
alternative_solution_2: Switch to a redundant sensor or controller immediately for every fault.
alternative_complexity_2: Fast failover when redundancy is healthy
alternative_2_tradeoff: Redundancy adds cost and common-mode failures; requires diagnostics and validated switching logic.
edge_cases: Stuck sensor; drifting sensor; bus timeout; power dip; watchdog reset; actuator saturation.
follow_up_questions: Add fault-tree analysis and worst-case execution-time proof.
